picks.excerpt: Nobel laureate Giorgio Parisi and Francesco Zamponi used Anthropic's Claude to crack a decade-old problem in jamming physics, proving why two parameters always sum to 1. The team reached a publishable proof in roughly 40 prompts, shifting their view of what LLMs can contribute to theoretical physics.
picks.rationale: Freshest item in the pool and the highest-actionability result: a Nobel laureate reaching a publishable proof in ~40 prompts is the strongest evidence yet that LLMs work as theory collaborators, not just search — physics/math sub-domain.

picks.excerpt: Researchers used AI to design synthetic RNA-guided nucleases with properties not found in nature, matching or exceeding the activity of natural CRISPR enzymes in cells. The Science paper lays out a strategy for generating non-natural genome-editing proteins from scratch.
picks.rationale: AI-designed editors that match or beat nature's own enzymes in live cells — a Science paper moving protein design from prediction to functional invention; life-science/genome-editing sub-domain.

picks.excerpt: Neural networks trained to spot biosignatures can be fooled into confidently misclassifying molecules that fall outside their training distribution. Researchers drove false-positive rates to 100% with as few as 150 modifications, arguing for human verification in life-detection missions.
picks.rationale: A 100% false-positive rate on biosignature detection is a hard limit on autonomous AI in life-detection missions — the counterweight to the pool's optimism, and the only astronomy/astrobiology item available.

picks.excerpt: Anthropic unveiled Claude Science, an AI application aimed at biopharma research labs. The piece frames it as a test of whether AI in the lab advances discovery rather than just trimming cost.
picks.rationale: A named product release aimed squarely at the research bench — the lab-automation/tooling angle, and a concrete tool readers can evaluate rather than a paper.

picks.excerpt: University of Illinois researchers found the brain begins deciding earlier than assumed, with primary sensory regions participating through feedback loops. The team frames it as a lesson for AI: feedforward CNN-style architectures may be missing a cheaper, biologically grounded design.
picks.rationale: Cognitive science that talks back to AI architecture — feedback loops as a cheaper design than feedforward stacks; the section's only neuroscience/cognition entry.
